units.body:
ELECTIONS: MEANING, FUNCTIONS AND TYPES

An election is a formal process through which eligible voters choose candidates or decide a public question. In representative government, elections give citizens a means of selecting people to exercise public authority for a defined term. They can provide political legitimacy, enable peaceful changes of leadership, make representatives answerable to voters and allow competing policies to be presented. Elections also help recruit political leaders and measure public support.

Elections may be general or by-election, direct or indirect, and may be held for executive or legislative offices. A credible election requires clear rules, an impartial administration, voter access, genuine competition, secret and secure voting where provided by law, accurate counting and a fair process for resolving disputes. An election is not automatically democratic merely because voting takes place; the process must protect choice and lawful participation.

TYPES OF VOTING AND FREE AND FAIR ELECTIONS

Voting systems describe how voters express a choice and how votes are counted. In an open ballot, a voter's choice is made publicly; this may make the process visible but can expose voters to pressure. In a secret ballot, the voter's choice is private, reducing intimidation and protecting independent judgement. Other voting methods may include voice voting, show of hands or electronic methods where authorised and properly secured.

A free and fair election allows eligible voters to participate without coercion and gives candidates a genuine opportunity to compete under impartial rules. Conditions include accurate voter registration, freedom to campaign peacefully, fair access to information, impartial election officials, secure voting materials, transparent counting, observation and lawful dispute resolution. The exact method should be assessed by whether it protects voters and produces a credible result.

ELECTORAL COMMISSION: MEANING, FEATURES AND FUNCTIONS

An electoral commission is an institution established by law to organise and supervise elections. In Nigeria, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) administers federal and state elections and performs other duties assigned by the Constitution and electoral legislation. Its independence, competence and impartiality are important because political competition is trusted only when the electoral process is administered fairly.

Typical functions include planning election timetables, registering eligible voters, registering political parties where authorised, conducting voter education, accrediting observers, organising polling and collation, announcing results and supporting lawful electoral processes. Important features include legal authority, operational independence, impartiality, transparency, adequate resources and accountability. A commission must follow the law and protect the rights of voters and candidates.

PUBLIC ADMINISTRATION: CIVIL SERVICE AND OVERSIGHT

Public administration is the organisation and management of government activities and public services. The civil service is the permanent body of officials who advise government, implement lawful policies, keep official records and provide continuity when elected leaders change. Civil servants are expected to act professionally, impartially, lawfully and in the public interest rather than as personal agents of a political office-holder.

The civil service is commonly organised into ministries, departments and agencies, with officers arranged in grades and levels of responsibility. The Civil Service Commission performs personnel functions assigned by law, such as appointments, promotion and discipline. An ombudsman or public complaints body investigates maladministration and helps citizens seek redress. Effective control combines clear rules, supervision, audits, legislative oversight, fair discipline and accessible complaint procedures.

PUBLIC CORPORATIONS: PURPOSE, STRUCTURE AND CONTROL

A public corporation is an organisation established or owned by government to provide a public service or manage an activity considered important to the public. It may operate with a separate legal identity and a governing board, while remaining accountable to the public authority that created it. Examples and legal forms differ by country and period, so students should use the examples given in the source and verify whether each organisation is still publicly owned.

Governments may establish public corporations to provide essential services, develop infrastructure, manage strategic resources or deliver services that may not be adequately supplied by private firms. Their structure may include a board, chief executive and operating departments. They differ from ordinary civil-service departments because they may have more operational autonomy and commercial responsibilities. Controls include legislation, ministerial supervision, audits, reporting, legislative scrutiny and performance review.

LOCAL GOVERNMENT: POWERS, FUNCTIONS AND CONTROL

Local government is the level of government closest to local communities. It is established by law to address local needs and provide services within its assigned area. Its functions may include local roads, markets, sanitation, community facilities, registration duties and support for primary services, subject to the Constitution and applicable laws. The actual division of responsibilities can change, so students should distinguish constitutional provisions from current administrative practice.

Local government can encourage grassroots participation because residents can raise concerns about nearby services and development projects. Its effectiveness depends on adequate funding, capable staff, transparent budgeting, public consultation and clear responsibilities. Problems may include weak revenue, political interference, corruption, poor planning and limited technical capacity. Controls include audits, lawful supervision, elected councils, public reporting and community monitoring.

PRE-COLONIAL HAUSA/FULANI AND IGBO POLITICAL SYSTEMS

Pre-colonial political systems were the institutions through which communities organised authority before colonial rule. In many Hausa/Fulani emirates, political authority was hierarchical, with an Emir exercising leadership alongside officials and councils within an established administrative and religious framework. The Sokoto Caliphate influenced political organisation in much of the north, although local arrangements varied between emirates.

Many Igbo communities were organised through decentralised institutions rather than a single central monarch. Authority could be shared among family heads, village assemblies, elders, age grades, titled persons and other community bodies. Decisions often depended on consultation and consensus, with different institutions performing social, judicial, economic or security roles. Avoid treating either system as identical everywhere: political organisation differed between communities and changed over time.

PRE-COLONIAL YORUBA POLITICAL SYSTEM

Pre-colonial Yoruba political organisation included kingdoms and towns with institutions that shared or balanced authority. In the Oyo Empire, the Alaafin was the central ruler, while the Oyo Mesi and other institutions exercised advisory, administrative and limiting functions. Other Yoruba kingdoms had their own arrangements and titles, so the Oyo structure should not be assumed to describe every Yoruba community.

Traditional rulers, councils of elders, chiefs, religious institutions, age grades and local associations could contribute to administration, dispute settlement, defence, ceremonies and community welfare. The relationship between the ruler and councils helped organise authority and, in some systems, restrain arbitrary decisions. Examination answers should identify the institution, state its role and explain how it contributed to governance rather than simply listing titles.

COLONIAL ADMINISTRATION IN AFRICA

Colonialism is the establishment and exercise of control by one state over another territory and its people. European colonial expansion in Africa was driven by a mixture of economic interests, strategic competition, political prestige, missionary activity and claims about cultural influence. Colonial rule took different forms across territories and changed over time; it should not be described as one identical system throughout Africa.

Colonial administration reorganised political authority, economic production, trade, education and infrastructure to serve the priorities of colonial powers. Some infrastructure and institutions created during colonial rule continued to be used after independence, but their development often reflected extraction and administrative control rather than equal local benefit. The effects included loss of sovereignty, boundary changes, economic dependence, new education systems and changes to existing institutions. Assess positive and negative effects separately and support each with examples.

BRITISH INDIRECT RULE AND FRENCH COLONIAL POLICIES

Indirect rule was a British colonial administrative approach that governed through existing traditional rulers and local institutions where colonial authorities considered them suitable. It was intended to reduce administrative costs, use established authority structures and make local administration easier. Its results differed by region: it often operated more readily in some northern emirates than in areas where authority was decentralised or where local institutions did not fit the system.

French colonial policy included assimilation and later association. Assimilation aimed to extend French language, institutions and aspects of French political culture to colonised populations, while association placed greater emphasis on governing through local conditions and institutions under French control. Neither approach meant that colonies had equal power with France. Compare the systems by examining local authority, citizenship, education, administration, cost and the degree of political control.

COLONIALISM: POSITIVE AND NEGATIVE IMPACTS

Colonialism affected West African societies in complex and unequal ways. Changes sometimes associated with colonial rule included expansion of formal schooling, new transport links, growth of towns, introduction of some modern administrative institutions and wider participation in international trade. These changes could create opportunities, but they were usually planned within a colonial system whose main authority and priorities lay outside the colonised territory.

Negative effects included loss of political independence, forced or unequal labour arrangements, extraction of resources, disruption of local economies, arbitrary boundaries, racial discrimination and the weakening or transformation of existing institutions. The benefits and costs were not shared equally. A balanced examination answer should avoid describing colonialism as wholly beneficial or wholly harmful without evidence; explain who gained, who lost and how the effects continued after independence.

NATIONALISM IN WEST AFRICA

Nationalism is a political movement or feeling that seeks self-government, independence or the advancement of a people regarded as a nation. In West Africa, nationalist activity grew through the work of educated elites, traditional leaders, workers, journalists, veterans, political associations and ordinary citizens. Nationalist organisations used newspapers, petitions, meetings, political parties and mass campaigns to challenge colonial authority.

Factors that encouraged nationalism included Western education, racial discrimination, economic hardship, urbanisation, growth of newspapers, labour organisation, the influence of returning soldiers and international support for self-determination. Nationalist movements differed in methods and objectives; some sought constitutional reform before demanding full independence. In examination answers, distinguish the meaning of nationalism from the factors that encouraged it and name leaders or organisations only where supported by the source.

NATIONALISM AFTER THE SECOND WORLD WAR

The Second World War accelerated demands for political change in Africa. African soldiers and workers gained new experiences, economic pressures increased, and international discussion of self-determination challenged the legitimacy of colonial rule. The Atlantic Charter and later international declarations helped nationalist leaders argue that people should have a voice in determining their political future, although colonial powers did not apply these principles consistently to their colonies.

Nationalist activity also expanded through trade unions, student groups, newspapers, political parties and mass campaigns. In some French West African territories, administrative policy and the political relationship with France shaped the pace and form of nationalist activity. Differences between colonies meant that independence campaigns did not follow one uniform path. Students should connect international events to local organisation, leadership and public mobilisation rather than treating one document as the sole cause of independence.

EARLY CONSTITUTIONAL DEVELOPMENT: 1914 COUNCIL AND NCBWA

Constitutional development describes changes in the legal and political arrangements through which a territory is governed. After the 1914 amalgamation of the Northern and Southern Protectorates, the Nigerian Council was established as an advisory body within the colonial administration. Its composition and powers did not amount to representative self-government; the governor and colonial authorities retained decisive control.

The National Congress of British West Africa (NCBWA) brought together educated West African representatives to demand constitutional reform, greater representation and political rights. It petitioned the British government and promoted political discussion across several colonies. The Council and the NCBWA were different in origin and purpose: one was part of the colonial administrative structure, while the other was a reform movement seeking greater African participation. Examination answers should identify their composition, authority and aims.

units.body:
CLIFFORD CONSTITUTION OF 1922

The Clifford Constitution came into operation in 1922 under Governor Sir Hugh Clifford. It created a Legislative Council for Southern Nigeria while the Northern Protectorate continued to be governed by proclamation from the Governor. The council had official and unofficial members; a limited number of Nigerian members were elected from Lagos and Calabar, while others were appointed. The Executive Council remained European in composition, so Nigerians had little influence over executive decisions.

The constitution introduced the elective principle into Nigerian politics and allowed more political activity, including the growth of political parties and newspapers. However, representation was restricted by geography, qualifications and the small electorate. It did not provide responsible government or equal participation for the whole country. Students should identify its composition, the limited elected representation, the position of the North and the political significance of the elective principle.

The Macpherson Constitution of 1951 followed wider consultations with Nigerians through village, district, provincial and regional processes. It expanded legislative participation and gave greater attention to regional representation. The 1953 constitutional conference considered further changes to Nigeria's federal structure and the transition towards self-government. The discussions addressed regional autonomy, the powers of central institutions, minority concerns and the future constitutional relationship between the regions and the centre. In examination answers, separate the features and achievements of the Macpherson Constitution from the decisions of the later conference.

LYTTLETON CONSTITUTION OF 1954

The Lyttleton Constitution of 1954 established a clearer federal structure for Nigeria, with a division of responsibilities between the central government and the regions. It strengthened regional institutions and recognised the country's diversity, while the federal government retained responsibility for matters assigned to it. The constitution was an important step in the development of Nigerian federalism before independence.

Its features included regional governments, a federal legislature and an allocation of legislative responsibilities. The arrangement gave regions more autonomy but also created challenges involving revenue, political rivalry, minority concerns and coordination between levels of government. For examination purposes, identify the provisions that made the system federal and explain both the gains and weaknesses. Do not confuse the 1954 constitution with the later independence or republican constitutions.

The London Constitutional Conference of 1957 and the Lagos Constitutional Conference of 1958 addressed the final arrangements for Nigeria's transition to independence. The discussions considered the structure of the federal government, the position of the regions, minority safeguards, the future of the legislature and the timetable for self-government. Constitutional conferences were negotiation forums rather than constitutions themselves: they produced recommendations and agreements that were later reflected in legal instruments. In examination answers, distinguish the issues discussed, the decisions reached and the constitutional provisions that were subsequently enacted.

INDEPENDENCE CONSTITUTION OF 1960

The 1960 Independence Constitution provided the legal framework for Nigeria's transition from British colonial rule to an independent state on 1 October 1960. It established constitutional institutions for a federal system and defined the roles of the head of state, head of government, legislature and courts. The monarch remained Nigeria's formal head of state, represented by a Governor-General, while the Prime Minister led the federal government.

The constitution preserved a parliamentary form of government and allocated responsibilities between federal and regional authorities. It was an important milestone because Nigeria became independent under a written constitutional arrangement, but some powers and institutional relationships continued to reflect the Westminster model. In examination answers, explain why it is called the Independence Constitution and identify its principal institutions without confusing the monarch, Governor-General and Prime Minister.

units.body:
FIRST REPUBLICAN CONSTITUTION OF 1963

The 1963 Republican Constitution ended Nigeria's formal constitutional relationship with the British monarch. The Queen ceased to be head of state and a Nigerian President became the ceremonial head of state and Commander-in-Chief. The President was elected by a joint sitting of the two federal legislative chambers, while the Prime Minister remained head of government under the parliamentary system.

The Supreme Court replaced the Privy Council as the final court of appeal in Nigeria, and the constitution strengthened the domestic role of the courts, including judicial review. It also adjusted the federal legislature and regional executive arrangements and contained provisions relating to fundamental rights and constitutional change. Its merits included greater constitutional independence and domestic final appeal; weaknesses included continued fusion of executive and legislative power under the parliamentary system and possible political instability from party competition.

units.body:
NIGERIAN FEDERALISM: ORIGIN

Federalism is a system of government in which constitutional powers are divided between a central authority and constituent units, with each level exercising authority within its assigned areas. Nigerian federalism developed from the country's amalgamation and later constitutional changes that recognised regional diversity and the need to share political authority. The 1914 amalgamation joined the Northern and Southern Protectorates, but the early administration remained largely unitary.

The federal system developed through constitutional reforms and the creation of regional governments, especially under the Lyttleton Constitution of 1954. The aim was to combine national unity with regional self-government. Federalism requires a written constitution, more than one level of government, a division of powers and institutions to resolve disputes. In examination answers, distinguish the early amalgamation from the later constitutional establishment of a federal system.

FACTORS, STRUCTURE AND PROBLEMS OF NIGERIAN FEDERALISM

Federalism may be adopted to manage diversity, protect regional interests, bring government closer to communities and prevent excessive concentration of power. In Nigeria, factors included differences in language, culture and history, the size of the country, regional identities and the desire to maintain unity while allowing local autonomy.

The federal structure includes a central government and subnational governments, with legislative and administrative powers allocated by the Constitution. The exclusive legislative list identifies matters reserved for the federal legislature; the concurrent list identifies matters on which both federal and state legislatures may legislate within constitutional limits. Problems can include disputes over revenue, resource allocation, political dominance, overlapping responsibilities, boundary disagreements and uneven development. A strong federal system needs clear rules, fair resource arrangements and respect for constitutional limits.

DEVELOPMENT OF EARLY POLITICAL PARTIES: NNDP, NYM AND NCNC

Political parties are organised groups that seek to influence or form government through elections and constitutional political activity. The Nigerian National Democratic Party (NNDP), associated with Herbert Macaulay, emerged in the early period of elective politics and contested seats under the Clifford Constitution. The Nigeria Youth Movement began as the Lagos Youth Movement and developed into a broader nationalist political organisation. It sought greater political participation and self-government.

The National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC) was formed in 1944, with Herbert Macaulay as its first president and Nnamdi Azikiwe as a prominent organiser and later leader. It campaigned for self-government and political education. These organisations differed in their origins, membership and political programmes, but each contributed to nationalist mobilisation. Use source-supported dates and leaders and distinguish the parties' aims from their electoral achievements.

units.body:
NORTHERN PEOPLE'S CONGRESS AND ACTION GROUP

The Northern People's Congress (NPC) developed from a socio-cultural association in Northern Nigeria and became a major political party in the 1950s. It was led by Sir Ahmadu Bello and had strong support in the Northern Region. Its programme focused on regional development, political autonomy and the interests of its supporters. Its political strength reflected the regional structure of Nigerian politics before and after independence.

The Action Group (AG) emerged from the Egbe Omo Oduduwa association and was led by Chief Obafemi Awolowo. It became a major party in Western Nigeria and promoted policies including education and social development. The parties differed in their regional bases, leadership, ideology and political programmes. Examination answers should compare their formation, aims, leadership and areas of influence without assuming that every member of a region supported the same party.

MINOR POLITICAL PARTIES AND SECOND REPUBLIC PARTIES

Nigeria's political history included parties with regional, ideological and national programmes. The United Middle Belt Congress (UMBC), associated with J.S. Tarka, advocated for the interests and political recognition of Middle Belt communities. The Northern Elements Progressive Union (NEPU), led by Aminu Kano, promoted political reform and challenged established power structures in Northern Nigeria.

During the Second Republic, parties included the National Party of Nigeria (NPN), Unity Party of Nigeria (UPN), Nigeria People's Party (NPP), Great Nigeria People's Party (GNPP) and People's Redemption Party (PRP). The Nigeria Advance Party (NAP) was registered later and contested the 1983 election. Parties differed in leadership, regional support and policy programmes. Students should use the source's party names and leaders accurately and distinguish First Republic from Second Republic organisations.

The Nigeria People's Party (NPP) was one of the major parties of the Second Republic and included prominent national political figures. The Great Nigeria People's Party (GNPP) emerged after a split involving party leadership and was associated with Alhaji Ibrahim Waziri. Party formation may result from shared ideology, regional interests, leadership disputes or disagreement about candidate selection. When studying these parties, identify their founders or leaders, aims, electoral participation and areas of influence, while avoiding unsupported claims about membership or results.

units.body:
KANO RIOT OF 1953 AND CENSUS CRISIS OF 1962/63

The Kano Riot of 1953 occurred amid political disagreement over the timing of self-government and tensions between northern and southern political leaders. A motion calling for self-government in 1956 and a counter-proposal contributed to political confrontation. Campaign activity and hostile exchanges increased tension, and violence in Kano worsened relations between political groups and raised concerns about national unity.

The 1962 census was criticised and cancelled, leading to a new census in 1963. Disputes about the accuracy and regional distribution of population figures created controversy because census results affected planning, representation and allocation of public resources. These crises show how political competition and distrust can destabilise institutions. Examination answers should separate immediate triggers from deeper causes and explain their political consequences.

WESTERN REGION ELECTION CRISIS OF 1965 AND ELECTION CRISES OF 1979/1983

The Western Nigeria election crisis of 1965 followed intense competition between the NNDP and UPGA-aligned candidates. Allegations of unfair nomination procedures, electoral malpractice, intimidation and disputed results created rival claims to political authority. Violence and disorder followed, weakening public confidence and contributing to the instability that preceded the January 1966 military coup.

The 1979 and 1983 elections took place under different constitutional arrangements. The 1979 election marked the return to civilian government under a presidential constitution, while the 1983 election was accompanied by allegations of rigging and widespread disputes. Election crises can arise from weak institutions, unfair competition, poor transparency and unresolved petitions. Students should distinguish the political context, electoral process and consequences of each crisis.

KADUNA STATE EXECUTIVE/LEGISLATIVE CRISIS OF 1981

The Kaduna State crisis arose after the People's Redemption Party (PRP) won the 1979 governorship election and Alhaji Balarabe Musa became governor. The National Party of Nigeria (NPN) held a majority of seats in the State House of Assembly. Under the constitutional process, the governor submitted nominees for appointment as commissioners, but the Assembly rejected the lists repeatedly. The disagreement strained relations between the executive and legislature.

The legislature later pursued impeachment proceedings against the governor, while attempts by other state assemblies to mediate did not resolve the conflict. The crisis illustrates the difficulties that can arise when the executive and legislature are controlled by opposing parties. Constitutional checks and balances are intended to ensure scrutiny and lawful appointments, but they can also produce deadlock if political rivalry replaces cooperation. Examination answers should identify the election result, the rejected commissioner nominees, the competing party control and the resulting impeachment dispute.
